_about: Krish's verdicts on titles, and what each teaches. Every title a reader sees first (article, YouTube, Shorts, cover, video title card, card headings) is written against these, offered to Krish as a few options, and used only once he has picked it: scripts/post-pack/title_check.py refuses an asset whose title has no 'picked' verdict here. Record a verdict with `title_check.py verdict`. Krish, 2026-10-14: 'figure out why I dislike it, and iterate, and understand what I actually like, and then encode that into the system forever.'

lessons.lesson: First, before legibility and every formula: every packaging line tells the piece's story in its series' lens. Start the round from the story (title_check.py lessons --plan prints it: his own statement in story.md, the outline's spine, the series' question) and judge each line by whether a reader would come away with THAT story. Fixing each line for the last complaint (legible, named, not shorthand) while losing the story gives lines that read fine and say the wrong thing: on 17 October 'Make Claude think harder' was a how-to tip on a mind.the.gap piece about the flood of AI releases and the choice about to be hidden from you.
lessons.from: Krish, 2026-10-17: "These are still awful. I'm getting exhausted. The story is about there being so many recent AI model releases and figuring out if that's actually important, why it's speeding up, and what choices a user is going to have to make (or what gears are going to be hidden from them in the future). It's a "mind the gap" piece remember. Why do I have to remind you about what this story is about?"

lessons.lesson: When his line is cut to fit a cover, card or title card, keep the words that carry its claim. 'ChatGPT and Claude: faster than ever' dropped 'releasing models' and so said the AIs are faster, which is not the piece's claim. If it will not fit, use a shorter line that keeps the claim ('New Claude. New ChatGPT.'), never a cut that changes it.
lessons.from: Krish, 2026-10-17: "Claude and ChatGPT are releasing models faster than ever. I don't think it's accurate to say that they are faster than ever. \"Does it even matter?\" is a better framing."

lessons.lesson: Above every formula and every surface: a stranger must understand the line in one second. It names a real thing people know (the product, the company, the person) in plain words, and says something true about it. Never the piece's own shorthand (low, high, gear, old and new, the badge): that is only legible to someone who has already watched it. makeyourmindup is not a famous channel, so a cryptic line reads as confusing, not intriguing, and a cheap one costs him the credibility the brand is built on. If a fresh reader cannot say what it is about and who it names, it never reaches him.
lessons.from: Krish, 2026-10-17: "Old beat new" and "who picked low" and you're on low are really stupid. This isn't a well-known concept and it's not a well-known media business. I can't release a Substack cover image that says you're on low. What the hell does that even mean? ... They're offensive to me. They hurt my soul. It's not as though I want to tweak it. It's that I am appalled that you keep bringing this shit to me.

lessons.lesson: Name the subject (Muse) in the title, then a more cryptic promise of what he reveals ('I break down ...'): the name is what people search and recognise; the promise is the open loop.

lessons.lesson: Name the product exactly as people would search it ('Meta's Muse AI'), never a vague stand-in ('Meta's new AI').

lessons.lesson: Never write a card heading or chapter divider to pass title_check's floor. Names stuffed in, label strings and bare numbers read as robotic. And never paste his words from the transcript either: that reads like a transcript, not a channel (Krish, 2026-10-17: "I do worry that using my own words for headings and chapter names will lose some of what makes this feel like a real media channel"). Write them the way a real media channel does (Johnny Harris, Vox, Jack Roberts): one device across the episode (numbered chapters or levels, one shape and length), each heading a short claim or promise that names the real thing, a small kicker with the source and date, built on the point he makes at that moment and his best phrases.
lessons.from: Krish, 2026-10-17: These headings are so stupid it's insane. I can't believe you're putting these to me. (27 Friday card and divider headings, all rejected)

verdicts.why: Same lesson: a headline built on one country reads as suspicion of that country; lead with sovereign AI and why countries want their own.
verdicts.krish: "IS YOUR AI CHINESE?" Sounds incredibly racist. The whole point of this is to understand what sovereign AI means and why countries are fighting to build their own AI as opposed to use another countries. We must not make this feel like we're stirring geopolitical hatred against China, it's just an example

verdicts.title: IS YOUR AI CHINESE?
verdicts.why: Never single out one country or its people in packaging: the story is why every country wants its own AI (sovereign AI), and China is one example inside it. Lead with the idea and name countries plural; a line that reads as 'is it foreign, is it suspect' is refused.
